text: The Appellant Jinpro International Inc. is a Guam business which imports products from the Philippines for resale to retail outlets on Guam. One product it imports is a packaged dried mango product known as 7D Dried Mangoes. The Appellant Western Sales Trading Company is another Guam company that imports a different brand of dried mangoes from the Philippines and competes directly with Jinpro in the sale of dried mangoes on Guam. Jinpro acquires its dried mango product from FPD Food International in the Philippines, which according to the trial court is a successor corporation to 7D Food International. Now, Jinpro was ordered by the Superior Court to turn over to Western Sales all of the dried mango product it had purchased from either FPD Food or 7D Food. This is a physical taking of Jinpro's private property. There are a whole host of organic ag and constitutional problems with this taking of Jinpro's dried mangoes. The simplest and most apparent is that just compensation must be paid for the taking. Just compensation in the circumstances of this case is fair market value, namely what a willing buyer would pay a willing seller for the mango product. This case that was submitted is especially simple, since we know what the fair market value is here, namely the amount for which Jinpro sells its dried mango product to its retail customers on Guam. However, the statute in question, 7GCA section 23401 FSEC, which was enacted in February 2018 and which I will refer to as a turnover statute, does not require the payment of fair market value, but only grants a lien to the condomnee, here Jinpro, in the amount of the condomnee's cost in the product. The problem is that the condomnee's cost in acquiring the asset under the law is not even relevant to the determination of just compensation, much less determination. This is the specific holding of a U.S. Supreme Court case, Olson v. United States, which I discuss in the briefs. This court need go no further. The turnover statute is inorganic and unconstitutional on its face by limiting the condomnee's compensation to the condomnee's cost in acquiring the asset taken as opposed to fair market value. But that is not the only problem with this strange statute. There is no assurance that the condomnee will actually receive even its cost in the asset taken. In the statute, all the condomnee gets is a lien for its cost in acquiring the asset, which lien is not paid unless and until the judgment creditor sells the asset. Now, I discuss the U.S. Supreme Court case, Williamson County, in the brief. Under that case, it is true that cash need not be paid at the time of the taking, but only if there is a certain and adequate provision. Here, the statute does not explicitly require that the condemned assets be sold, much less at any time for their sale. And what if the amount realized at a sale is less than the condomnee's cost? Then what? The turnover statute plunks miserably the requirement that there be a certain and adequate provision for the payment of just compensation and is inorganic and unconstitutional for this reason also, as if that were not enough. The statute...
